Augustine: free choice of the will.front: What is the luck objection to Augustine's uncaused evil will?
Augustine: free choice of the will.back: If **nothing explains** why the will turned, the turning looks like **chance**, not control.

Reading: Augustine, Confessions XI, on w.back: "**If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not**" (Pusey).

Reading: Augustine, Confessions XI, on w.front: Augustine's three times, in the soul
Reading: Augustine, Confessions XI, on w.back: A present of things past (**memory**), of things present (**sight**), of things future (**expectation**). Confessions XI.20.
**A stretching-out of the mind**: Augustine's guess at what time is (Pusey: "protraction"), Confessions XI.26.

Augustine: the City of God and the two c.back: **Two loves**: the earthly city by love of self to the contempt of God; the heavenly by love of God to the contempt of self (*City of God* XIV.28).
Without justice, kingdoms are **great robber bands**: the pirate with one ship is called a robber, Alexander with a fleet an emperor (IV.4).
**The tranquillity of order** (*City of God* XIX.13).

Boethius: the Consolation of Philosophy.back: About **480–524 or 525**. Roman senator, consul 510; executed under **Theodoric** near Pavia. Translated Aristotle's logic.
Written in prison; **Lady Philosophy** consoles him in five books of **prose and verse**. Never mentions Christ.

Boethius: the Consolation of Philosophy.front: State Boethius's argument that Fortune's goods cannot make us happy
Boethius: the Consolation of Philosophy.back: A good you **can lose** leaves you fearing its loss; so happiness lies in a good that **cannot be lost**: the highest good, God.

Boethius: God's foreknowledge and human.back: "**The possession of endless life whole and perfect at a single moment**" (*Consolation* V, tr. James). Not mere endless duration.
**Simple**: men are necessarily mortal. **Conditional**: if you know someone is walking, he must be walking; the knowing does not **force** the walk.

Boethius: God's foreknowledge and human.front: How does Boethius answer the foreknowledge problem?
Boethius: God's foreknowledge and human.back: God does not *fore*know; he **sees all at once** in his eternal present, so his knowledge imposes only **conditional** necessity.

Boethius and Porphyry: the problem of un.back: Porphyry, about **234–about 305**, Plotinus's pupil. The *Isagoge* introduces Aristotle's *Categories* and **raises three questions about genera and species**.

Boethius and Porphyry: the problem of un.front: State Porphyry's three questions about universals
Boethius and Porphyry: the problem of un.back: Do genera and species exist **in reality or only in the mind**? If real, **bodies or not**? **Apart from** sensible things or **in** them?
Considering apart what is **together in reality** is not false (a line without its body). Universals **subsist in sensibles and are understood apart** from them.

John Philoponus: the world had a beginni.back: About **490–about 570**, Alexandria. *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World* (**529**). Also anticipated **impetus**.
If the past were infinite, an **infinite series of days** would have been gone through to reach today; an infinite cannot be traversed; so the past is **finite**.

John Philoponus: the world had a beginni.front: What is the modern objection to Philoponus's addition argument?
John Philoponus: the world had a beginni.back: Since **Cantor**, an infinite set can be **added to without growing** in number; so "adding a year to an infinite past" is not absurd.

Pseudo-Dionysius: negative theology as p.back: Syrian author writing about **500** under the name of Paul's convert. Shown in **1895** (Koch, Stiglmayr) to borrow from **Proclus**.
**Cataphatic**: speaking of God by affirmation. **Apophatic**: by negation. Plus eminence, *hyper-*: "super-good".

Pseudo-Dionysius: negative theology as p.front: What is the self-refutation objection to Pseudo-Dionysius's negative theology?
Pseudo-Dionysius: negative theology as p.back: "Nothing can be said of God" is **itself said of God**. Reply: the negations are **a ladder**, a practice, not a thesis.

Maximus the Confessor: the natural will.back: About **580–662**. Opposed **Monothelitism** (one will in Christ); mutilated and exiled; vindicated **680–681**.

Maximus the Confessor: the natural will.front: Maximus: does the will belong to nature or to person?
Maximus the Confessor: the natural will.back: To **nature**: every rational nature has a **natural will**. The person determines **how** it is used.
The **deliberating** will (*gnōmē*): weighing and hesitating because we **do not see the good clearly**. A sign of freedom's **limits**, not its height.

Eriugena: the Periphyseon and the divisi.back: About **800–about 877**, Irish, at **Charles the Bald**'s court. Translated **Dionysius** into Latin; *Periphyseon* about 864–866.

Eriugena: the Periphyseon and the divisi.front: State Eriugena's four divisions of nature
Eriugena: the Periphyseon and the divisi.back: Creates, not created (**God as source**); creates and created (**primordial causes**); created, not creating (**the world**); neither (**God as end**).
**Disputed.** Condemned **1225**. He insists God transcends creation; many now say **panentheist** at most.

Anselm: the ontological argument of the.back: Contains the **ontological argument**. Anselm (1033–1109), abbot of Bec, Archbishop of Canterbury. Motto: **faith seeking understanding**.

God is **that than which nothing greater can be conceived**; it is in the understanding; existing **in reality is greater**; so if it were only in the mind a greater could be conceived. So it **exists in reality**.

Anselm: the ontological argument of the.front: What is Kant's objection to Anselm's argument?
Anselm: the ontological argument of the.back: **Existence is not a real predicate**: it adds nothing to a concept; a hundred real thalers contain no more than a hundred imagined.

Gaunilo's lost island and Anselm's reply.front: Gaunilo of Marmoutier, *On Behalf of the Fool*
Gaunilo's lost island and Anselm's reply.back: Monk who replied to Anselm **soon after the *Proslogion*** (1077–1078); Anselm had the objection **copied with the *Proslogion***.

Gaunilo's lost island and Anselm's reply.front: What is Gaunilo's lost island objection?
Gaunilo's lost island and Anselm's reply.back: The same form "proves" an island **more excellent than all lands**; so **the form is bad**.

Gaunilo's lost island and Anselm's reply.front: How does Plantinga answer Gaunilo's island?
Gaunilo's lost island and Anselm's reply.back: Island-greatness has **no intrinsic maximum** (always one more palm tree), so "the greatest possible island" is **incoherent**; divine greatness has a maximum.

Falsafa: Greek philosophy goes into Arab.back: Arabic borrowing of *philosophia*: philosophy **in the Greek tradition**. Distinct from ***kalam***, dialectical theology.
**809–873**, Nestorian Christian physician; the greatest translator, often **Greek to Syriac to Arabic**.

Falsafa: Greek philosophy goes into Arab.front: What were the *Theology of Aristotle* and the *Liber de causis*, really?
Falsafa: Greek philosophy goes into Arab.back: Not Aristotle: the first a paraphrase of **Plotinus**, the second a reworking of **Proclus**. So Arabic "Aristotle" came **Neoplatonised**.

Al-Kindi: the first philosopher of the A.back: About **800–about 870**, Baghdad; "**the philosopher of the Arabs**". *On First Philosophy*, dedicated to al-Mu'tasim.

Al-Kindi: the first philosopher of the A.front: State al-Kindi's argument against an actual infinite body
Al-Kindi: the first philosopher of the A.back: Remove a finite part: if the rest is infinite, **part equals whole**, absurd; if finite, the whole is finite. So the world is **finite in time**.

Al-Kindi: the first philosopher of the A.front: Al-Kindi on truth from foreign sources
Al-Kindi: the first philosopher of the A.back: We should **not be ashamed to take truth from wherever it comes**, even foreign peoples; to argue against philosophy is to **do** philosophy.

Al-Farabi: the Second Teacher and the vi.back: About **870–950 or 951**, Baghdad and Damascus. "**The Second Teacher**" after Aristotle. *The Virtuous City*.
**Grammar** rules one language; **logic** rules thought in every language.

Al-Farabi: the Second Teacher and the vi.front: Al-Farabi: how does religion relate to philosophy?
Al-Farabi: the Second Teacher and the vi.back: Religion gives **in images and persuasion** the truths philosophy **proves**: it is an **imitation** of philosophy, for the many.

Avicenna: essence, existence and the nec.back: **980–1037**, born near Bukhara. *The Cure* (*al-Shifa'*); *Canon of Medicine*. Read Aristotle's *Metaphysics* **forty times**.

Avicenna: essence, existence and the nec.front: Avicenna's distinction of essence and existence
Avicenna: essence, existence and the nec.back: **What** a thing is versus **that** it is. One can know a phoenix's essence without knowing it exists, so in creatures existence **comes from outside**.

Avicenna: essence, existence and the nec.front: State Avicenna's proof of the necessary existent
Avicenna: essence, existence and the nec.back: Possible things need a cause; the **whole collection** of possibles is possible and needs a cause **outside** it; that cause is **necessary in itself**. Works **even if the world is eternal**.

Avicenna: the flying man.back: A man created **fully formed in the air**, sight veiled, limbs apart, sensing nothing, would still **affirm that he exists**, but not that he has a body. So the self is **not the body**.

Avicenna: the flying man.front: What is the masked man objection to Avicenna's flying man?
Avicenna: the flying man.back: From "I know X" and "I do not know Y" it **does not follow that X ≠ Y**: knowing depends on presentation.
A **pointer** or reminder, not a strict proof: how Avicenna himself frames the flying man.

Al-Ghazali: the Incoherence of the Philo.back: Twenty discussions against the *falasifa*. Al-Ghazali, **1058–1111**. Three views called unbelief: **eternal world**, God knowing only universals, no **bodily resurrection**.

Al-Ghazali: the Incoherence of the Philo.front: State al-Ghazali's argument on cause and effect
Al-Ghazali: the Incoherence of the Philo.back: We observe **fire, then burning**: co-occurrence, not necessary connection. Fire without burning is not contradictory; **God creates** the burning.

Al-Ghazali: the Incoherence of the Philo.front: Al-Ghazali's reply on creation at one moment rather than another
Al-Ghazali: the Incoherence of the Philo.back: That is what a **will** is: a power to choose between **equal options**; and there was **no time before** creation.

Averroes: the Incoherence of the Incoher.back: **1126–1198**, Córdoba; judge and physician. "**The Commentator**" on Aristotle. *Incoherence of the Incoherence* (about 1180).

Averroes: the Incoherence of the Incoher.front: Averroes's reply to al-Ghazali on causation
Averroes: the Incoherence of the Incoher.back: To deny necessary causes is to deny **knowledge itself**: knowing a thing is knowing its causes.
The **material intellect**, which receives universal ideas, is **one for all humans** (*Long Commentary on the De anima*). Attacked by Aquinas, 1270.

Averroes: the Incoherence of the Incoher.front: Averroes's *Decisive Treatise*: three kinds of people
Averroes: the Incoherence of the Incoher.back: **Demonstrative**, **dialectical**, **rhetorical**. Where proof conflicts with scripture's apparent sense, **interpret** scripture.

Saadia Gaon: reason and revelation in Je.back: **882–942**, born in Egypt; Gaon of **Sura** from 928. *The Book of Beliefs and Opinions* (**933**).

Saadia Gaon: reason and revelation in Je.front: Saadia: why revelation, if reason can find the truth?
Saadia Gaon: reason and revelation in Je.back: **Speed**; for those who **cannot follow the proofs**; and **certainty** while the proof is worked out.
From **finitude**, **composition**, **accidents**, and **time** (an infinite past cannot be traversed).

Maimonides: the Guide of the Perplexed a.front: *The Guide of the Perplexed* — Maimonides, about 1190
Maimonides: the Guide of the Perplexed a.back: Written in Arabic in Cairo. Maimonides, **1138–1204**, born in Córdoba.

Maimonides: the Guide of the Perplexed a.front: State Maimonides's argument for negative attributes
Maimonides: the Guide of the Perplexed a.back: God is **absolutely simple**; a positive attribute would add something to his essence and make him **many**; so only **negations** and **attributes of action** are true of God.
Each person learns one more thing a ship is **not**; the tenth has **almost the correct notion**. So proven negations bring us **nearer to God**.

Maimonides: the Guide of the Perplexed a.front: Maimonides on the eternity of the world
Maimonides: the Guide of the Perplexed a.back: **Neither creation nor eternity can be demonstrated**; he accepts creation, and would reinterpret scripture if eternity were proved.

The road into Latin Europe: Toledo, the.front: Toledo, as a centre of translation
The road into Latin Europe: Toledo, the.back: Taken by Castile in **1085**; from the **1130s** the chief centre of **Arabic-to-Latin** translation.
About **1114–1187**; translated some **seventy** works from Arabic: the *Almagest*, Aristotle's *Physics*, Avicenna's *Canon*, the *Liber de causis*.

The road into Latin Europe: Toledo, the.front: Why did the Latins think al-Ghazali was a philosopher?
The road into Latin Europe: Toledo, the.back: Only his *Aims of the Philosophers*, a **summary of Avicenna**, was translated, usually **without the preface** saying he meant to refute it.

The road into Latin Europe: Toledo, the.front: The Paris ban on Aristotle's natural philosophy
The road into Latin Europe: Toledo, the.back: **1210** synod; repeated in the **1215** statutes. By **1255** all of Aristotle was required.

Looking back: what late antiquity and th.front: The three positions on the world's beginning, Philoponus to Maimonides
Looking back: what late antiquity and th.back: **Provably created** (Philoponus, al-Kindi, Saadia); **eternal** (Avicenna, Averroes); **neither provable** (Maimonides, later Aquinas).

Looking back: what late antiquity and th.front: Al-Ghazali and Averroes on causation: the open question
Looking back: what late antiquity and th.back: Is there **necessary connection** in nature (Averroes), or only regular succession **sustained by God** (al-Ghazali)? Hume reopens it.

Context: cathedral schools, universities.back: Philosophy done by **professional teachers in the schools and universities**, about **1100 to 1450**, by a fixed method of question and disputation.
A **guild of masters and students**; **Bologna** and **Paris** first, about 1200, then Oxford. Faculties: **arts, theology, law, medicine**.

Context: cathedral schools, universities.front: Why did the Latin translations of Aristotle shake the medieval schools?
Context: cathedral schools, universities.back: Within about a century, from about 1150, **almost all of Aristotle** arrived with Avicenna's and Averroes's commentaries: a complete philosophy that seemed to teach an **eternal world** and a soul that might not survive.

The problem of universals: realism, nomi.back: Do genera and species **exist or only in the mind**? Are they **bodies or not**? Do they exist **apart from or in** sensible things? Porphyry left them unanswered.

The problem of universals: realism, nomi.front: State the medieval problem of universals as a dilemma
The problem of universals: realism, nomi.back: **Knowledge is general**, so something general seems real; but **everything that exists is individual**, and one thing wholly in many would be in two places with contrary properties.
From *nomen*, name: **only individuals exist**; universals are **words or signs**.

Roscelin, William of Champeaux and Abela.back: Early nominalist, known only through enemies: universals a **breath of the voice**. Recanted at **Soissons, 1092**.

Roscelin, William of Champeaux and Abela.front: Abelard's refutation of William of Champeaux's material essence realism
Roscelin, William of Champeaux and Abela.back: If the whole essence **animal** is in Socrates and in a donkey, the **same thing is rational and non-rational** at once: a contradiction.
What makes "man" true of Socrates: his **being a man**, which Abelard insists is **not a thing**.

Abelard: the ethics of intention.front: Abelard's Know Yourself (Scito te ipsum, late 1130s)
Abelard: the ethics of intention.back: Abelard's ethics: **sin is consent** to what one believes wrong; the deed adds nothing to guilt.

Abelard: the ethics of intention.front: Why does Abelard say the outward deed adds nothing to guilt?
Abelard: the ethics of intention.back: Blame is only for what is **in our power**; feelings arise unbidden and deeds depend on circumstance, but **consent is fully ours**.

Abelard: the ethics of intention.front: What is the objection to Abelard's ethics of intention?
Abelard: the ethics of intention.back: It makes the **sincere persecutor blameless**. Abelard: society may still punish deeds; critics: we can be **culpable for our beliefs**.
"Yes and No": **conflicting authorities** set side by side on 158 questions, with rules for reconciling them.

Peter Lombard's Sentences and the schola.back: Four books of patristic opinions by topic; **the theology textbook** from the 1220s to the 1500s. Every master **had to comment on it**.

Peter Lombard's Sentences and the schola.front: State the five parts of a scholastic quaestio
Peter Lombard's Sentences and the schola.back: **Whether...**; **objections** ("It seems that"); **on the contrary** (*sed contra*); **I answer that** (*respondeo*); **replies** to each objection.
A public disputation "on **whatever you like**": anyone could put any question to the master.

The recovery of Aristotle and the condem.back: Bishop **Stephen Tempier** of Paris condemns **219 propositions** (eternity of the world, one intellect, limits on God's power). Kilwardby condemns an Oxford list on **18 March**.

The recovery of Aristotle and the condem.front: State the Duhem thesis about the 1277 condemnation, and the reply
The recovery of Aristotle and the condem.back: Duhem: by insisting God could make a vacuum or many worlds, 1277 **freed physics from Aristotle**. Reply: most historians think this **overstated**.
The Latin name for **Averroes** (died **1198**), whose commentaries came with Aristotle.

Bonaventure: illumination, and why the w.front: Bonaventure's The Mind's Road to God (1259)
Bonaventure: illumination, and why the w.back: *Itinerarium mentis in Deum*, by the Franciscan **Bonaventure** (about 1217 to 1274).

Bonaventure: illumination, and why the w.front: State Bonaventure's argument for divine illumination
Bonaventure: illumination, and why the w.back: Certain knowledge is of the **unchangeable**; our minds and objects are **changeable**; so certainty needs an **unchangeable light**, God's eternal reasons.

Bonaventure: illumination, and why the w.front: State Bonaventure's traversal argument against an eternal world, and Aquinas's reply
Bonaventure: illumination, and why the w.back: An infinite past **cannot have been traversed** to reach today. Aquinas: an infinite past has **no starting point** to traverse from; the beginning is **known by faith, not proof**.

Albert the Great: Aristotle for the Lati.back: German Dominican, **teacher of Aquinas** at Cologne; paraphrased nearly all Aristotle. The **Universal Doctor**.
Each discipline by **its own methods**: the natural philosopher asks what happens **by natural causes**, not what God could do by miracle.
A nature **before the thing** (God's idea), **in the thing** (its real nature), **after the thing** (our concept).

Aquinas: faith, reason, and what each ca.back: **Thomas Aquinas** (1224/25 to **1274**): his vast teaching work, in thousands of articles; **unfinished**.
Truths about God **reason can prove** (that God exists, is one); distinct from **articles of faith** (the Trinity), known only by revelation.

Aquinas: faith, reason, and what each ca.front: State Aquinas's argument that faith and reason cannot conflict
Aquinas: faith, reason, and what each ca.back: Both come from **God, who is truth**; truth cannot contradict truth; so any argument against faith is **not a true demonstration**.

Aquinas: essence and existence.front: Aquinas's On Being and Essence (about 1252 to 1256)
Aquinas: essence and existence.back: *De ente et essentia*: argues that in all things but God **essence and existence are really distinct**.
I can know **what a phoenix is** without knowing **whether it exists**; so existence is not part of essence, except in one being whose **essence is to exist**: God.

Aquinas: essence and existence.front: What is the main objection to Aquinas's real distinction of essence and existence?
Aquinas: essence and existence.back: It shows only a **distinction in our concepts**, not a **real** one in things. Also, after Kant and Frege, **existence is not a property**.

Aquinas: the Five Ways set out.front: Name Aquinas's Five Ways (Summa I q.2 a.3)
Aquinas: the Five Ways set out.back: From **motion**, **efficient cause**, **possibility and necessity**, **gradation**, and **governance** (things acting for ends).

Aquinas: the Five Ways set out.front: Why does Aquinas's First Way not rule out an infinite series in time?
Aquinas: the Five Ways set out.back: Its regress is of an **essentially ordered** (*per se*) series, like **hand, staff, stone**, where each acts now only through the first. He allowed a temporal infinite regress possible.

Aquinas: the Five Ways set out.front: What is the quantifier-shift objection to Aquinas's Third Way?
Aquinas: the Five Ways set out.back: From "**each** thing at some time does not exist" it infers "at some time **nothing** exists": invalid, like "everyone has a mother, so one woman mothers all".

Reading: Aquinas, the Five Ways (Summa t.front: The two objections Aquinas puts first in Summa I q.2 a.3
Reading: Aquinas, the Five Ways (Summa t.back: The **problem of evil** (infinite goodness would destroy evil) and **sufficiency** (nature and human will explain everything).

Reading: Aquinas, the Five Ways (Summa t.front: How does Aquinas's First Way define motion?
Reading: Aquinas, the Five Ways (Summa t.back: "The **reduction of something from potentiality to actuality**": any change, as **fire makes wood actually hot**.

Reading: Aquinas, the Five Ways (Summa t.front: English Dominican translation of the Summa (1920)
Reading: Aquinas, the Five Ways (Summa t.back: "Literally translated by Fathers of the English Dominican Province", **Second and Revised Edition, 1920**; on New Advent and Gutenberg.

Aquinas on analogy: how human words can.front: Why does Aquinas say words for God are neither univocal nor equivocal?
Aquinas on analogy: how human words can.back: **Univocal** would make God one finite instance of a kind; **equivocal** would make God-talk empty. So they are **analogical**.
Said of animal (**has** health), medicine (**causes** it), urine (**signs** it): meanings **ordered to one**.

Aquinas on analogy: how human words can.front: Cajetan's On the Analogy of Names (1498)
Aquinas on analogy: how human words can.back: Systematised Aquinas on analogy; whether it **distorts Aquinas** is disputed (McInerny).

Aquinas: the soul as the form of the bod.back: A substance is **matter organised by form**; the human soul is **the substantial form of the body**: one substance, not two.

Aquinas: the soul as the form of the bod.front: State Aquinas's argument that the human soul subsists
Aquinas: the soul as the form of the bod.back: The intellect knows the natures of **all bodies**, so it **uses no bodily organ**; a thing acts as it is; so the soul has **being of its own** and survives death.
**One** substantial form in a human, the rational soul, giving bodiliness, life, sense and reason. Opposed by Franciscans; a related thesis condemned at **Oxford, 1277**.

Aquinas: natural law and the virtues.front: Aquinas's first precept of natural law (I-II q.94 a.2), paraphrased
Aquinas: natural law and the virtues.back: **Good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided**: self-evident, as non-contradiction is in thought.

Aquinas: natural law and the virtues.front: What is the is-ought objection to Aquinas's natural law?
Aquinas: natural law and the virtues.back: It seems to infer **ought** from our **inclinations**. Reply: reason **grasps the goods as self-evidently good**; inclinations only show them.

Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist.back: Paris arts master, leader of the **Latin Averroists**; views condemned **1270**; died at **Orvieto**. Dante puts him in **Paradise**.

Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist.front: State the Averroist argument for the unity of the intellect
Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist.back: The intellect grasps universals, so is **immaterial**; matter is what makes many of one kind; so there is **one intellect for all humans**.

Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist.front: What is Aquinas's chief objection to Siger's one intellect?
Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist.back: Experience: **this human thinks**. If the intellect were one separate thing, it would not be *I* who understand. *On the Unity of the Intellect*, **1270**.

Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist.front: Did Siger of Brabant hold a "double truth"?
Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist.back: **The standard view: no.** He said conclusions **follow from Aristotle's principles**, while the simple truth is with faith.

Duns Scotus: the univocity of being and.back: Scottish Franciscan, the **Subtle Doctor**; Oxford, Paris, died **Cologne 1308**. Main work: the **Ordinatio**.

Duns Scotus: the univocity of being and.front: State Scotus's argument from doubt for the univocity of being
Duns Scotus: the univocity of being and.back: One can be **certain God is a being** while **doubting** whether finite or infinite; so *being* is a concept **distinct from both and common** to God and creatures.
Between **formalities** in one thing, distinct in definition **before any act of mind** but **inseparable**: God's justice and mercy.

Duns Scotus: haecceity, and the will tha.back: "**Thisness**" (Latin *haec*): a positive principle making a thing **this individual**; formally distinct from its common nature.

Duns Scotus: haecceity, and the will tha.front: Why does Scotus reject matter as the principle of individuation?
Duns Scotus: haecceity, and the will tha.back: Matter is **itself general** until something makes it *this* matter; the question just **recurs**.

Duns Scotus: haecceity, and the will tha.front: Scotus's two affections of the will
Duns Scotus: haecceity, and the will tha.back: **Affection for the advantageous** (one's own happiness) and **affection for justice** (a good loved **for itself**), from Anselm.

Ockham: the razor and nominalism.back: English Franciscan, the **Venerable Inceptor**; *Summa of Logic* (about **1323**); fled Avignon **1328**; died in **Munich**.
**Do not posit more things than necessary**; necessity means **self-evidence, experience, or Scripture**. The Latin slogan is a later formula.

Ockham: the razor and nominalism.front: State Ockham's argument against Scotus's formal distinction
Ockham: the razor and nominalism.back: A distinction outside the mind makes **two things** (separable by God); one only in the mind leaves the thing **simply singular**; there is **no third option**.
Concepts are **natural signs** of individuals, combined into mental sentences; a universal is a sign of **many**.

Ockham: God's absolute and ordained powe.back: **Absolute**: all God **could** do without contradiction. **Ordained**: the order God **has chosen**. One power, two ways of considering it.

Ockham: God's absolute and ordained powe.front: State Ockham's argument for intuitive cognition of a non-existent
Ockham: God's absolute and ordained powe.back: The act of seeing is a **thing distinct** from the star; God could keep the act **without the star**; so one could intuit a star that **does not exist**.

Ockham: God's absolute and ordained powe.front: What is the Euthyphro objection to Ockham's ethics?
Ockham: God's absolute and ordained powe.back: If God could make **hatred of God** right, goodness is God's **whim**; if not, goodness seems **prior to God's will**.

John Buridan: the via moderna in the art.back: Paris **arts master** for over thirty years, never a theologian; *Summulae de dialectica*; nominalist logician.
A **spinning top** keeps turning in place, where air cannot push it; so the air does not move projectiles; the thrower gives an **impetus**.
**No**: not in his surviving works; probably a **critics' parody**. Aristotle has a man **equally hungry and thirsty**.
What a term **stands for** in a sentence: men, the concept, or the word ("Man has three letters").

Byzantine philosophy: Photios, Psellos a.back: Summaries and judgements of **279 books** by **Photios** (about 810 to about 893), twice patriarch of Constantinople.
Byzantine courtier and historian (*Chronographia*); "**consul of the philosophers**"; reviver of **Plato, Plotinus and Proclus**.

Byzantine philosophy: Photios, Psellos a.front: Why was John Italos condemned in 1082?
Byzantine philosophy: Photios, Psellos a.back: For teaching **pre-existent souls**, an **eternal world** and the **Forms**; the *Synodikon* condemned accepting Greek doctrines **as true**, not only as training.

Palamas and Barlaam: the hesychast contr.back: Athonite monk, archbishop of Thessaloniki; *Triads* (about **1338 to 1341**); upheld at councils of **1341, 1347, 1351**.
God's **essence** is unknowable and unshared; his **energies** are **uncreated**, truly God, and **participable** by creatures.

Palamas and Barlaam: the hesychast contr.front: What is Barlaam's objection to Palamas's energies?
Palamas and Barlaam: the hesychast contr.back: A real distinction in God makes **a simple God composite**, or two Gods. Palamas: the energies are **of** the essence, as rays of the sun.

Nicholas of Cusa: learned ignorance and.front: Nicholas of Cusa's On Learned Ignorance (1440)
Nicholas of Cusa: learned ignorance and.back: *De docta ignorantia*, by **Nicholas of Cusa** (1401 to 1464), cardinal from 1448.

Nicholas of Cusa: learned ignorance and.front: State Cusanus's argument for learned ignorance
Nicholas of Cusa: learned ignorance and.back: We know by **proportion**; between finite and infinite there is **none**; so God cannot be known by comparison, but we can **know that and why we do not know**.
*Coincidentia oppositorum*: in the infinite, opposites **coincide**; the infinite circle is a **straight line**; God is maximum and minimum.

Looking back: the via antiqua, the via m.front: Via antiqua and via moderna (15th century)
Looking back: the via antiqua, the via m.back: The **old way** (Aquinas, Albert, Scotus; realism) against the **modern way** (Ockham, Buridan; nominalism), taught in rival universities.
King **Louis XI** banned nominalist teaching at Paris in **1474**; lifted **1481**.

Looking back: the via antiqua, the via m.front: Name three questions the schoolmen left open for the Renaissance
Looking back: the via antiqua, the via m.back: Any three: **universals**; **analogy or univocity** in talk of God; **individuation**; the soul's relation to the body; **will versus intellect**.

Context: Europe from the Renaissance to.back: The view that **reason alone, without the senses, can give substantial knowledge** of reality. Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz.
The view that **all knowledge of the world comes from experience**. Bacon and Hobbes lean this way; Locke, Berkeley, Hume (Stage 9).

Context: Europe from the Renaissance to.front: Why did the wars of religion press early modern philosophers towards certainty?
Context: Europe from the Renaissance to.back: If reasonable people kill each other over doctrine (Thirty Years' War **1618–48**), philosophy needed **a foundation for knowledge and peace** that did not depend on contested authority.

Humanism and the revival of Plato: Ficin.back: Florentine (**1433–1499**); first complete **Latin translation of Plato** (printed **1484**); *Platonic Theology*; credited with **"Platonic love"**.

Humanism and the revival of Plato: Ficin.front: Pico della Mirandola, *Oration on the Dignity of Man*
Humanism and the revival of Plato: Ficin.back: Written **1486** for his **900 theses**; printed after his death. Humans have **no fixed nature** and can shape themselves, down to beasts or up to angels.

Humanism and the revival of Plato: Ficin.front: Lorenzo Valla and the Donation of Constantine
Humanism and the revival of Plato: Ficin.back: Valla (1407–1457) showed by its anachronistic Latin that the Donation was a **forgery** (**1440**): humanist philology as a weapon.

Machiavelli: The Prince and the effectua.back: Written **1513**, printed **1532**, by Niccolò Machiavelli (**1469–1527**), ex-secretary of the Florentine republic.

Machiavelli: The Prince and the effectua.front: Machiavelli: is it better to be loved or feared?
Machiavelli: The Prince and the effectua.back: **Safer to be feared** than loved if one must choose (ch. 17): fear depends on the prince, love on the subjects. But **never be hated**.
*Virtù*: **energy, skill, boldness**, not moral virtue. *Fortuna*: chance, a **flooding river** held back by dykes built in calm weather.
Machiavelli sets **pagan civic morality against Christian morality** and shows they **cannot both be lived**: values can genuinely conflict (1972).

Montaigne and the new scepticism.back: Michel de Montaigne (**1533–1592**); books I–II **1580**, book III **1588**. *Essai* = "attempt". The key sceptical essay is the **"Apology for Raymond Sebond"** (II.12).
**"What do I know?"**: his motto, with the emblem of a **balance in equilibrium**: Pyrrhonian suspension of judgement.
**Faith over reason because reason fails** to reach truth. Montaigne's position: keep the religion one was born into and receive faith as a gift.

Montaigne and the new scepticism.front: Montaigne's regress argument against a criterion of truth
Montaigne and the new scepticism.back: The senses need checking by reason; reason needs checking by further reasoning, **and so without end**. So we have **no criterion that does not beg the question**.

Bacon: the idols and the new induction.back: Francis Bacon (**1561–1626**), **1620**: the "new instrument", named against Aristotle's *Organon*.
The **ant** only collects; the **spider** spins from itself; the **bee** gathers and transforms: true science.
Tables of **presence, absence and degree**, then **exclusion**; negative instances weigh most. Result (the "first vintage"): **heat is a kind of motion**.

The scientific revolution's challenge to.back: Nature is **matter in motion**: all change explained by the size, shape and motion of particles. Descartes, Gassendi, Hobbes, **Boyle**.

The scientific revolution's challenge to.front: Galileo on tastes, smells and colours
The scientific revolution's challenge to.back: They exist **only in the perceiver**; size, shape, number and motion are in things. Later called **secondary and primary qualities** (Boyle, Locke).

The scientific revolution's challenge to.front: What did the new science expel from Aristotle's physics?
The scientific revolution's challenge to.back: **Final causes** (goals) and **substantial forms**; and the Earth at rest at the centre.

Descartes: the method of doubt and the e.back: René Descartes (**1596–1650**), **1641**, printed with **Objections and Replies**.
There are **no sure signs by which waking can be told from sleep**, so any particular perception might be a dream. Arithmetic survives it.

Descartes: the method of doubt and the e.front: Why does Descartes invent the evil demon?
Descartes: the method of doubt and the e.back: To keep **hyperbolic doubt** alive even about **mathematics** and his body: a powerful deceiver who makes him err about everything.
Doubt **deliberately exaggerated** beyond any sensible person's, used **once** as a tool to test foundations.

Descartes: the cogito and the thinking t.back: "I think, therefore I am": *Discourse* Part IV (**1637**, in French); the Latin in the *Principles* (**1644**). The *Meditations* say **"I am, I exist"**.
**A thinking thing**: one that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, refuses, imagines and **seems to perceive**.

Descartes: the cogito and the thinking t.front: What is Lichtenberg's objection to Descartes's cogito?
Descartes: the cogito and the thinking t.back: We should say **"it thinks"**, as "it lightens": **thinking is certain; a single, lasting "I" is not**.
**Disputed.** Descartes: a **simple intuition**, not a syllogism. Hintikka (1962): a **performance** that refutes its own denial.

Reading: Descartes's Meditation II, the.back: Every sensed quality of the wax changes by the fire, yet **the same wax remains**; so it is known as **extended, flexible, movable**, by **the mind alone**.

Reading: Descartes's Meditation II, the.front: Descartes's hats and cloaks from the window
Reading: Descartes's Meditation II, the.back: We say we *see* men, but see only hats and cloaks that might cover machines: **we judge, and call it seeing**.
In Meditation II he wants, like Archimedes, **one point firm and immovable**: one certainty to build on.

Descartes: the trademark argument for Go.back: The reality an idea **represents**, as opposed to its **formal reality** as a mental event.
I have an idea of an **infinite** being; a cause must have **at least as much reality** as its effect, including what an idea represents; I am finite; so **only an infinite God** could cause it.

Descartes: the trademark argument for Go.front: What is Hobbes's objection to Descartes's trademark argument?
Descartes: the trademark argument for Go.back: **We have no idea of God**, only a word or images of finite things; "infinite" means only "not finite".

Descartes: the ontological argument.back: God is **supremely perfect**; **existence is a perfection**; so existence belongs to God's essence, as **valley to mountain** or angle-sum to triangle.

Descartes: the ontological argument.front: What is Caterus's objection to Descartes's ontological argument?
Descartes: the ontological argument.back: It shows only that **the concept** of God includes existence, not that anything real answers to it.

Descartes: the ontological argument.front: What is Gassendi's objection to Descartes's ontological argument?
Descartes: the ontological argument.back: **Existence is not a perfection**, but the condition of having any; Kant (1781): **"being" is not a real predicate**.

Descartes: the Cartesian circle.back: Arnauld's objection (**Fourth Objections, 1641**): clear perceptions are trusted because God exists, and God's existence because of clear perceptions.
**Whatever I clearly and distinctly perceive is true**, guaranteed by a God who is **no deceiver**.

Descartes: the Cartesian circle.front: Descartes's reply to the Cartesian circle
Descartes: the Cartesian circle.back: **Present** clear perceptions cannot be doubted while attended to; God is needed for conclusions **remembered** without their proofs. Whether this works is **disputed**.
The view that knowledge rests on **basic beliefs needing no support**, with the rest built on them. Descartes is its classic exponent.

Descartes: mind-body dualism and the rea.front: State Descartes's conceivability argument for dualism
Descartes: mind-body dualism and the rea.back: I can **clearly and distinctly conceive** mind without body; whatever I so conceive apart **God can make exist apart**; so **mind is really distinct** from body.
Body is **divisible**; the mind is not (no half a mind); so they are not the same thing.

Descartes: mind-body dualism and the rea.front: What is Arnauld's triangle objection to Descartes's dualism?
Descartes: mind-body dualism and the rea.back: One can conceive a right triangle **without** conceiving the Pythagorean property, yet it cannot lack it: **what is conceived apart may not be apart**.
The view that there are **two fundamentally different kinds of substance**: minds (essence: **thought**) and bodies (essence: **extension**).

Descartes: the pineal gland and Elisabet.back: Princess (**1618–1680**); her letters to Descartes from **May 1643** posed the **interaction problem**; the *Principles* (1644) were dedicated to her.

Descartes: the pineal gland and Elisabet.front: State Elisabeth of Bohemia's objection to Descartes
Descartes: the pineal gland and Elisabet.back: Bodies move only by **contact**; contact needs **extension**; the soul is unextended; so **how can it move the body?**

Descartes: the pineal gland and Elisabet.front: Why did Descartes choose the pineal gland?
Descartes: the pineal gland and Elisabet.back: It is **single** (not paired), **central**, and **mobile** among the cavities where animal spirits flow.
**Thought**, **extension**, and **the union** of mind and body, which is known best **through the senses and ordinary life**.

Gassendi, Arnauld and the Objections and.back: Priest and astronomer (**1592–1655**); revived **Epicurean atomism** for Christians; author of the **Fifth Objections**; an empiricist.
Port-Royal theologian (**1612–1694**); **Fourth Objections**; co-author of the ***Port-Royal Logic*** (1662).
Any act shows existence. Descartes: only if it is a **thought**, a **seeming** to walk.
Minim friar (**1588–1648**), centre of Europe's learned letters; **circulated the *Meditations*** and gathered the Objections.

Hobbes: materialism and the mechanical m.back: English philosopher (**1588–1679**); ***Leviathan*** **1651**; materialist; wrote the **Third Objections** to Descartes.
Imagination is **"decaying sense"**; reasoning is **reckoning**, adding and subtracting names.
The view that **freedom and determinism are compatible**. Hobbes: liberty is the **absence of external impediments**.

Hobbes: materialism and the mechanical m.front: Hobbes and Bramhall, *Of Liberty and Necessity*
Hobbes: materialism and the mechanical m.back: Published **1654**: Hobbes's compatibilism against Bishop **John Bramhall**, who held blame requires real alternatives.

Hobbes: the state of nature, the social.front: Life in Hobbes's state of nature
Hobbes: the state of nature, the social.back: A war of **every man against every man**; life **"solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short"**.
Everyone covenants with everyone to give their right of self-government to a **sovereign** who is **not party to the contract**; "Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words".

Hobbes: the state of nature, the social.front: What is Locke's objection to Hobbes's sovereign?
Hobbes: the state of nature, the social.back: Escaping polecats and foxes by being **devoured by lions**: an absolute sovereign is a **greater danger** than one's neighbours.

Pascal: the wager.back: French mathematician and philosopher (**1623–1662**); founded **probability** with Fermat (**1654**); ***Pensées*** printed **1670**.
You **must** bet; reason cannot decide; a **non-zero chance of infinite gain** outweighs any finite cost; so **wager that God is**.

Pascal: the wager.front: What is the many-gods objection to Pascal's wager?
Pascal: the wager.back: There are **many possible gods**, some punishing Christian belief, so the two-column table is **incomplete** (Diderot).

Pascal: the wager.front: Pascal's answer to "I cannot believe at will"
Pascal: the wager.back: **Act as if you believe**, go to Mass, use holy water: **belief follows habit**.

Pascal: the Pensées and the reasons of t.front: What does Pascal mean by "the heart"?
Pascal: the Pensées and the reasons of t.back: **A power of immediate knowing**, not emotion: we know **first principles** (space, time, number) by the heart, not by proof.
Man is **"a thinking reed"**: the feeblest thing in nature, yet nobler than the universe that crushes him, because **he knows he dies**.

Pascal: the Pensées and the reasons of t.front: Pascal's *esprit de géométrie* and *esprit de finesse*
Pascal: the Pensées and the reasons of t.back: The **geometrical** mind reasons from few clear principles; the **intuitive** mind grasps many subtle ones at a glance.
Our pastimes **distract us from our condition**: unhappiness comes from being unable to **stay quietly in one's room**.

Spinoza: substance monism and Deus sive.back: Baruch Spinoza (**1632–1677**); "demonstrated in geometrical order"; printed **posthumously, 1677**.
**"God or Nature"**: the one infinite substance, not a person outside the world.

Spinoza: substance monism and Deus sive.front: State Spinoza's argument for substance monism
Spinoza: substance monism and Deus sive.back: No two substances share an attribute; God has **all** attributes and necessarily exists; so **besides God no substance can be conceived** (I.14).

Spinoza: substance monism and Deus sive.front: What is Leibniz's objection to Spinoza's monism?
Spinoza: substance monism and Deus sive.back: Two substances might **share one attribute and differ in another**: proposition 5 does not rule them out.

Spinoza: the geometric method, determini.back: Each thing's **striving to persist in its own being** (III.6), its very essence; in humans, conscious **desire**.
Stronger than determinism: **the world, laws included, could not have been otherwise** (*Ethics* I.33).
A stone pushed into motion, if conscious, would think it moved **freely**; so do we, **aware of our desires, ignorant of their causes**.
**Acting from one's own nature, understood**: understanding a passion weakens its hold; the summit is the **intellectual love of God**.

Spinoza: the Tractatus Theologico-Politi.back: Published **anonymously, 1670**; banned in Holland **1674**; defends the **freedom to philosophise**.
**Interpret the Bible from the Bible alone**, like nature from nature: language, history, authorship.

Spinoza: the Tractatus Theologico-Politi.front: Spinoza on the purpose of the state
Spinoza: the Tractatus Theologico-Politi.back: **Freedom**: thought cannot be commanded, so a state that tries breeds **hypocrites and rebels**.

Malebranche and occasionalism.back: Oratorian priest (**1638–1715**); ***The Search after Truth*** (**1674–75**); occasionalism and **vision in God**.
**God is the only true cause**; created "causes" are only **occasions** on which God acts by general laws.
A true cause is one with a **perceived necessary connection** to its effect; we perceive this only with **God's will**; so only God truly causes.

Malebranche and occasionalism.front: What is Leibniz's objection to Malebranche's occasionalism?
Malebranche and occasionalism.back: It makes nature **a perpetual miracle**, God intervening at every instant.

Leibniz: monads and pre-established harm.back: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (**1646–1716**); written **1714**, printed after his death.
A **simple, unextended substance** whose only states are **perceptions and appetitions**; it mirrors the whole universe; it **has no windows**.
Enlarge a thinking machine and walk inside as into a mill: you find only **parts pushing parts**, never **a perception**. So perception is not mechanical.
Mind and body **never interact**; God set them up so their states **always correspond**, like **two perfectly made clocks**.

Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea.back: **Nothing is without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise** (*Monadology* 32).

Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea.front: Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles vs Leibniz's Law
Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea.back: **Identity of indiscernibles**: things alike in every property are one (disputed). **Leibniz's Law** (indiscernibility of identicals): one thing shares all its properties (accepted).

Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea.front: What is Max Black's objection to Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles?
Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea.back: A universe of **two exactly similar spheres** (1952): nothing distinguishes them, yet there are **two**.

Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea.front: Leibniz's truths of reason and truths of fact
Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea.back: **Reason**: necessary, opposite contradictory, finite analysis. **Fact**: contingent, opposite possible, **infinite analysis** only God completes.

Leibniz: the best of all possible worlds.back: **1710**; Leibniz's reply to **Bayle** on evil; he coined "theodicy": **the justification of God**.

Leibniz: the best of all possible worlds.front: State Leibniz's argument for the best possible world
Leibniz: the best of all possible worlds.back: God chooses among **infinitely many possible worlds**; he needs a **sufficient reason**; for a perfect being only **the best** suffices; so this is the best.

Leibniz: the best of all possible worlds.front: What is the "no best world" objection to Leibniz?
Leibniz: the best of all possible worlds.back: For any world there may be **a better**, as for any number a larger; then **no world is the best** and the argument fails.

Leibniz and Clarke: space, God and the c.back: **1715–16**, five letters each, via **Caroline, Princess of Wales**; Clarke for Newton; published **1717**.

Leibniz and Clarke: space, God and the c.front: State Leibniz's shift argument against absolute space
Leibniz and Clarke: space, God and the c.back: If space were absolute, God could have placed the universe elsewhere; the worlds would be **indiscernible**; God would have **no sufficient reason**; so space is **relational**.

Leibniz and Clarke: space, God and the c.front: Clarke's reply to Leibniz on sufficient reason
Leibniz and Clarke: space, God and the c.back: **God's will alone** can be a sufficient reason: a free agent may choose between **equal options**.
Newton's God must **wind up his watch from time to time**: a poor workman. Clarke: that is **providence**, not repair.

Anne Conway: one substance, alive throug.front: Anne Conway, *Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy*
Anne Conway: one substance, alive throug.back: Conway (**1631–1679**); Latin **1690** (Amsterdam), English **1692**; posthumous and anonymous.

Anne Conway: one substance, alive throug.front: Anne Conway on body and spirit
Anne Conway: one substance, alive throug.back: **Not two substances but two ends of a scale**: body is condensed spirit; all creatures **live and perceive**.

Anne Conway: one substance, alive throug.front: Anne Conway's argument against Descartes's dualism
Anne Conway: one substance, alive throug.back: If spirit and body were **wholly different**, they **could not affect each other**; they do; so they **share one nature**.

Looking back: from Renaissance doubt to.front: Six early modern answers to the mind-body problem
Looking back: from Renaissance doubt to.back: **Descartes** interaction; **Hobbes** only body; **Malebranche** God causes; **Spinoza** one substance, two attributes; **Leibniz** harmony; **Conway** one living substance.

Looking back: from Renaissance doubt to.front: Which early modern problem waited for Hume?
Looking back: from Renaissance doubt to.back: **Causation**: Malebranche's point that we never **perceive necessary connection** between events.

Context: the new science, a bloodless re.back: The view that **all ideas and knowledge of the world come from experience**.
**1688–89**: James II replaced by William and Mary; Parliament limits the crown. The background to Locke's politics.

Context: the new science, a bloodless re.front: Why is "British empiricists versus continental rationalists" only a rough label?
Context: the new science, a bloodless re.back: It is a **later historians' scheme**: none of them saw himself on a team, Locke relied heavily on reason, and Leibniz valued experience.

Locke: the attack on innate ideas.back: Published December **1689** (dated 1690); Book I attacks **innate ideas**, Book II derives all ideas from experience.

Locke: the attack on innate ideas.front: State Locke's argument against innate principles from universal consent
Locke: the attack on innate ideas.back: If innate, **everyone would assent**; children and whole nations do not; so none is innate. And consent could be explained otherwise anyway.

Locke: the attack on innate ideas.front: What is the objection to Locke from Leibniz's veined marble?
Locke: the attack on innate ideas.back: The mind is not blank but like **marble with veins**: ideas are innate as **dispositions** that experience brings out (*New Essays*, written about 1704, published 1765).

Locke: simple and complex ideas, and whe.back: **Sensation** (outside things) and **reflection** (the mind noticing its own operations).
**Simple**: one unanalysable appearance, received passively. **Complex**: built by the mind — **modes, substances, relations**.
**Nominal**: the features by which we sort a kind (yellow, heavy). **Real**: the hidden particle structure that causes them.

Locke: simple and complex ideas, and whe.front: What is the veil-of-ideas objection to Locke?
Locke: simple and complex ideas, and whe.back: If we perceive only our **ideas**, we can never check them against the world. (Whether Locke held such a view is **disputed**: Yolton says no.)

Locke: primary and secondary qualities,.back: **Solidity, extension, shape, motion or rest, number**: our ideas of them **resemble** the body.
**Colour, sound, taste, smell, heat**: only **powers** in bodies to cause sensations; the ideas do **not resemble** anything in them.
Warm one hand, chill the other, dip both in the same water: it feels **hot and cold at once**, so the heat felt is **in us**.

Locke: primary and secondary qualities,.front: Locke on substance: "something, I know not what"
Locke: primary and secondary qualities,.back: We suppose a **support** of qualities but have **no clear idea** of it — like the Indian's tortoise under the elephant.

Locke: personal identity and memory.back: **Sameness of consciousness**: a person reaches as far back as consciousness (memory) extends — not same body, not same soul.
The prince's soul and memories enter the cobbler's body: **same man** to others, but **the person is the prince**.

Locke: personal identity and memory.front: What is Reid's brave officer objection to Locke?
Locke: personal identity and memory.back: General remembers officer, officer remembers flogged boy, general forgets boy: by Locke general = boy and ≠ boy. **Identity is transitive**, so the simple memory theory fails (**1785**).

Locke: personal identity and memory.front: What is Butler's circularity objection to Locke on identity?
Locke: personal identity and memory.back: Real memory **presupposes** identity, so it cannot constitute it (**1736**). Reply: **quasi-memory**.

Molyneux's problem: would the newly sigh.back: A man born blind who knows cube and sphere **by touch** is made to see: can he tell which is which **by sight alone, before touching**?
Dublin scientist (**1656–1698**), *Dioptrica Nova* (1692); his question printed in Locke's *Essay*, **2nd edition 1694**.

Molyneux's problem: would the newly sigh.front: Who answered Molyneux's question yes, and who no?
Molyneux's problem: would the newly sigh.back: **No**: Molyneux, Locke, Berkeley. **Yes**: Leibniz. Held et al. (**2011**): not at first, but learned **within days**.

Locke: the Two Treatises, property and t.back: Anonymous, **1689** (dated 1690). The First refutes **Filmer**; the Second: state of nature, property, consent, resistance.
You own your person and so your labour; what you **mix your labour with** becomes yours, if **enough and as good** is left and nothing **spoils**.

Locke: the Two Treatises, property and t.front: What is Hume's objection to Locke's tacit consent?
Locke: the Two Treatises, property and t.back: Staying in a country is no more consent than a man carried **aboard a ship asleep** consents by not leaping into the sea ("Of the Original Contract", 1748).

Locke: the Two Treatises, property and t.front: Locke's argument for toleration, and Proast's reply
Locke: the Two Treatises, property and t.back: **Force cannot produce belief**, so persecution is useless. Proast (1690): force can make people **consider** arguments.

Berkeley: immaterialism and esse est per.back: "**To be is to be perceived**" — of sensible things (*Principles*, **1710**).
Only **minds and their ideas** exist; tables and trees are collections of ideas, not unthinking matter.
"**An idea can be like nothing but an idea**" — so ideas cannot resemble unperceived matter.

Berkeley: immaterialism and esse est per.front: What is Moore's act–object objection to Berkeley?
Berkeley: immaterialism and esse est per.back: Berkeley confuses the **mental act** of perceiving blue with the **blue perceived**, which need not be mental (**1903**).

Berkeley: the master argument and God as.back: Try to conceive a tree **unconceived**: in doing so you **conceive it**. So nothing can be conceived to exist unconceived.

Berkeley: the master argument and God as.front: What is the standard objection to Berkeley's master argument?
Berkeley: the master argument and God as.back: It confuses conceiving **a tree as unconceived** (content) with the tree **being conceived by me** (act).
I cannot choose what I see, so ideas of sense are caused by **another spirit**; their regular order is the **laws of nature**.

Hume: impressions, ideas and the copy pr.back: Books 1–2 **1739**, Book 3 **1740**; recast as the *Enquiry concerning Human Understanding* (**1748**) and the *Enquiry concerning the Principles of Morals* (1751).

Hume: impressions, ideas and the copy pr.front: Hume's impressions and ideas: the difference
Hume: impressions, ideas and the copy pr.back: Differ in **force and vivacity**: impressions are lively sensations and feelings; ideas their **fainter copies**.
Every simple idea is **copied from a simple impression**. Test of meaning: "from what impression is that supposed idea derived?"
One could imagine an unseen shade between seen ones — a **counterexample** to the copy principle that Hume himself raises and sets aside.

Hume's fork: relations of ideas and matt.back: All objects of reason are **relations of ideas** (certain, known by thought) or **matters of fact** (probable, known by experience).

Hume's fork: relations of ideas and matt.front: Why can no reasoning prove that the sun will rise tomorrow, according to Hume?
Hume's fork: relations of ideas and matt.back: It is a matter of fact: "**the contrary of every matter of fact is still possible**" — its denial implies no contradiction.

Hume's fork: relations of ideas and matt.front: What is the self-refutation objection to Hume's fork?
Hume's fork: relations of ideas and matt.back: The fork is neither true by definition nor learned from experience, so by its own test it goes **"to the flames"**.

Hume: causation, constant conjunction an.front: Why can't Hume find an impression of necessary connection?
Hume: causation, constant conjunction an.back: In one case we see only **one event, then another**; reason allows the effect's absence; we don't know how the will moves limbs.
Events of one kind **regularly followed** by events of another; after it, **custom** makes the mind expect the second.
(1) an object followed by another, all similar objects followed by similar; (2) one whose appearance **conveys the thought** to the other.
Reading (Wright, **Galen Strawson 1989**) on which Hume believed in **real causal powers** we cannot know — against the regularity reading.

Reading: Hume's Enquiry, section IV, on.back: Inference from experience assumes **nature is uniform**; that cannot be **demonstrated** (its denial is conceivable) nor shown by **experience** without **circularity**.
If reason drew inductive conclusions, **one case would do as well as a hundred**; but only long experience gives firm expectation — so it is **custom**.

Reading: Hume's Enquiry, section IV, on.front: Three replies to Hume on induction
Reading: Hume's Enquiry, section IV, on.back: **Strawson**: reasonable by definition. **Reichenbach**: the best bet. **Popper**: science needs no induction. None generally accepted.

Hume: the self as a bundle of perception.front: Hume's argument against a substantial self
Hume: the self as a bundle of perception.back: Looking within he always finds **some particular perception**, never a simple, constant self; so no impression, so no idea.
A person is "**a bundle or collection of different perceptions**" in perpetual flux (*Treatise* 1.4.6, 1739).

Hume: the self as a bundle of perception.front: What is the objection to Hume's bundle theory from "who is looking"?
Hume: the self as a bundle of perception.back: The search for the self **presupposes a searcher**; and perceptions seem to need an **owner**.

Hume: scepticism, and nature's cure for.back: Nature, not reason: "**I dine, I play a game of backgammon**, I converse, and am merry with my friends".
Keep belief but hold it **modestly**, confined to **common life and experience** — versus unliveable Pyrrhonism.

Hume: scepticism, and nature's cure for.front: The sceptical and naturalist readings of Hume
Hume: scepticism, and nature's cure for.back: **Sceptical**: empiricism ruins knowledge. **Naturalist** (**Kemp Smith**): basic beliefs come from instinct, not reason, and are none the worse.

Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and Butler: the m.back: Against Hobbes: we have **natural affections** for others and a reflective **sense of right and wrong**.
A faculty like sight that **approves benevolence** regardless of our interest (*Inquiry*, **1725**).

Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and Butler: the m.front: State Butler's argument against psychological egoism
Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and Butler: the m.back: Pleasure comes from **satisfying a desire for an object**, so desire for the object comes first; not all desire is for one's own pleasure (**1726**).

Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and Butler: the m.front: What is the rationalist objection to Hutcheson's moral sense?
Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and Butler: the m.back: Had we been made differently, **cruelty would have been right**: morality becomes a fact about our wiring (Balguy, **Price 1758**).

Hume: reason the slave of the passions,.front: Hume's argument that reason alone cannot move us
Hume: reason the slave of the passions,.back: Reason finds **relations of ideas and facts**; neither moves without a desire; so "**reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions**".
Moralists slide from **is** to **ought**; Hume asks how the new relation can be **deduced** from wholly different ones (*Treatise* 3.1.1).
Not natural but a **convention**, arising because everyone gains from respecting property.

Hume on miracles.back: No testimony suffices unless **its falsehood would be more miraculous** than the fact it reports (*Enquiry* X, **1748**).

Hume on miracles.front: Hume's four historical arguments against miracle reports
Hume on miracles.back: Too few **reliable witnesses**; love of **wonder**; origin in **"ignorant and barbarous nations"**; **rival religions'** miracles cancel.

Hume on miracles.front: What is the question-begging objection to Hume on miracles?
Hume on miracles.back: Calling experience **"uniform"** against miracles assumes every miracle report is false — the point at issue (**Campbell, 1762**).

Hume's Dialogues: the argument from desi.back: Written in the **1750s**, published **1779**; Cleanthes (design), Demea (faith), Philo (sceptic).

Hume's Dialogues: the argument from desi.front: State Cleanthes' design argument in Hume's Dialogues
Hume's Dialogues: the argument from desi.back: The world is like **one great machine**; machines come from minds; like effects, like causes; so the world's cause is **like a mind**.

Hume's Dialogues: the argument from desi.front: Philo's objections to design, in Hume's Dialogues
Hume's Dialogues: the argument from desi.back: **Weak analogy** (animal or plant?); **one universe**; **who designed the designer**; many gods; **chance over time**; **evil**.

Thomas Reid: common sense against the wa.front: Reid's *Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense*
Thomas Reid: common sense against the wa.back: **1764**. Blames scepticism on the **theory of ideas**; defends direct perception.

Thomas Reid: common sense against the wa.front: Reid's diagnosis of Berkeley and Hume
Thomas Reid: common sense against the wa.back: Their scepticism follows from the unproved **way of ideas**; an argument ending in absurdity refutes its **premise**.

Thomas Reid: common sense against the wa.front: Reid's parity argument against the sceptic
Thomas Reid: common sense against the wa.back: Reason and the senses come from the **same constitution**: no ground to trust one and doubt the other.

Voltaire and Diderot: the French Enlight.back: **1759**: satire of Leibnizian optimism after the **Lisbon earthquake (1755)**; ends "cultivate our garden".
Protestant **Jean Calas** executed **1762** on a false charge; Voltaire's *Treatise on Toleration* (1763) won his rehabilitation (1765).
With **d'Alembert**, **1751–72**: 17 volumes of text, 11 of plates; banned 1759, finished in secret.

Voltaire and Diderot: the French Enlight.front: Did Voltaire say "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it"?
Voltaire and Diderot: the French Enlight.back: **No**: written by **Evelyn Beatrice Hall** in **1906** to sum up his attitude.

Rousseau: the state of nature and the or.front: Rousseau's *Discourse on the Origin of Inequality*
Rousseau: the state of nature and the or.back: **1755**: natural man solitary and compassionate; inequality is a **product of society**.
**Amour de soi**: natural self-concern. **Amour-propre**: self-love that depends on **others' esteem** — born of comparison.

Rousseau: the state of nature and the or.front: Rousseau's objection to Hobbes's state of nature
Rousseau: the state of nature and the or.back: Hobbes painted **civilised** man and called him natural: pride and greed need **society** to exist.

Rousseau: the general will, the Social C.back: **1762**: "Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains." Legitimacy through the **general will**.

Rousseau: the general will, the Social C.front: Rousseau's general will versus the will of all
Rousseau: the general will, the Social C.back: **Will of all**: sum of private wants. **General will**: what each wills **as citizen** for the common good.

Rousseau: the general will, the Social C.front: What is the totalitarian objection to Rousseau, and the reply?
Rousseau: the general will, the Social C.back: "**Forced to be free**" licenses crushing dissent (Talmon, Berlin). Reply: the general will must be **general in source and object**, so cannot single anyone out.
**1762**: natural, **negative** education; the Savoyard Vicar; Book V's **Sophie**, educated to please men.

Adam Smith: sympathy and the impartial s.front: *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* — Adam Smith
Adam Smith: sympathy and the impartial s.back: **1759**, revised to the **6th edition (1790)**; morality from **sympathy** and the **impartial spectator**.
We judge ourselves by imagining a **well-informed, disinterested** observer; internalised as conscience, "the man within".

Adam Smith: sympathy and the impartial s.front: Adam Smith's earthquake in China example
Adam Smith: sympathy and the impartial s.back: A European would sleep after hearing of millions dead, yet would **never sacrifice them to save his little finger** — conscience, not love, restrains him.
Supposed clash of **sympathy (1759)** and **self-interest (1776)**; most scholars now see **no real contradiction**.

Burke and Wollstonecraft: tradition, rev.front: *Reflections on the Revolution in France* — Burke
Burke and Wollstonecraft: tradition, rev.back: **November 1790**; against abstract rights, for **inherited institutions**; society a partnership of living, dead and unborn.

Burke and Wollstonecraft: tradition, rev.front: State Burke's case against the French Revolution
Burke and Wollstonecraft: tradition, rev.back: Society is too complex to redesign; tradition holds **tested wisdom**; abstract rights know no limits; so **reform, don't revolutionise**.

Burke and Wollstonecraft: tradition, rev.front: *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman* — Wollstonecraft
Burke and Wollstonecraft: tradition, rev.back: **1792**: virtue needs reason, women are rational, so women must be **educated** and independent.
"I do not wish them to have **power over men; but over themselves**."

Looking back: what the empiricists settl.front: Which problems did Hume leave open for Kant?
Looking back: what the empiricists settl.back: **Causation, induction, the self**, and whether morals rest on **feeling or reason**.

Looking back: what the empiricists settl.front: Kant's way between rationalism and empiricism
Looking back: what the empiricists settl.back: Knowledge **begins with** experience, but the mind supplies the **forms** (space, time, cause) that make experience possible (*Critique of Pure Reason*, **1781**).

Context: Prussia, the Enlightenment and.back: Systematiser of **Leibniz**; his rationalist metaphysics was the **standard German university philosophy** Kant was trained in.
King **1740–1786**; allowed unusual freedom to publish, so long as his subjects **obeyed**.

Context: Prussia, the Enlightenment and.front: The question that pressed on Kant's generation
Context: Prussia, the Enlightenment and.back: **Can reason know anything beyond experience**, and if not, what becomes of **God, freedom and morality**?

Kant's life, the pre-critical years and.back: Born **22 April 1724**, died **12 February 1804**, both in **Königsberg**; professor of logic and metaphysics from **1770**.

Kant's life, the pre-critical years and.front: Kant's *Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens* (1755)
Kant's life, the pre-critical years and.back: Pre-critical work proposing the **nebular hypothesis**: the solar system formed from a rotating cloud.

Kant's life, the pre-critical years and.front: Kant's 'dogmatic slumber': who woke him, and where he said so
Kant's life, the pre-critical years and.back: **Hume**, on causation; in the **Prolegomena (1783)**. A 1798 letter to Garve credits the **antinomies** instead.
About **1770–1781**: almost nothing published while he wrote the *Critique of Pure Reason*.

Kant's Copernican turn in the Critique o.back: First edition **1781 (A)**, revised **1787 (B)**; cited by both paginations, e.g. A51/B75.
Instead of assuming knowledge conforms to objects, assume **objects (as we know them) conform to our cognition**: then a priori knowledge of them is explicable.
**Transcendental**: about the conditions that make knowledge of objects possible. **Transcendent**: beyond all possible experience.

Kant's judgments: analytic and synthetic.front: Kant's analytic and synthetic judgments, with his examples
Kant's judgments: analytic and synthetic.back: **Analytic**: predicate contained in subject ('All bodies are extended'). **Synthetic**: predicate adds to it ('All bodies are heavy').

Kant's judgments: analytic and synthetic.front: Why did Kant think 7 + 5 = 12 is synthetic a priori?
Kant's judgments: analytic and synthetic.back: The concept of the sum contains only **joining 7 and 5**, not 12; you must **count in intuition**. Yet it is **necessary**.

Kant's judgments: analytic and synthetic.front: What is the objection to Kant from geometry?
Kant's judgments: analytic and synthetic.back: **Non-Euclidean geometries** and **general relativity (1915)** suggest Euclid is not necessarily true of physical space. Reply: Kant meant **perceptual** space.

Kant's Transcendental Aesthetic: space a.back: A representation relating **directly to a single object**; ours are all **sensible**.

Kant's Transcendental Aesthetic: space a.front: Kant: space is empirically real and transcendentally ideal. Meaning?
Kant's Transcendental Aesthetic: space a.back: Everything we can experience **is** in space; but space belongs to **our form of perceiving**, not to things in themselves.

Kant's Transcendental Aesthetic: space a.front: What is Trendelenburg's 'neglected alternative' to Kant?
Kant's Transcendental Aesthetic: space a.back: Space might be a form of our intuition **and also** a feature of things in themselves; Kant has not ruled this out.
Left and right hands: alike in every inner measure, yet **not superposable**; the difference shows only **relative to space as a whole**.

Kant's categories and the Transcendental.front: Kant: 'Thoughts without content are void; intuitions without conceptions, blind'
Kant's categories and the Transcendental.back: Knowledge needs **both** sensibility (intuitions) and understanding (concepts). Meiklejohn's translation, 1855.
Four groups of three: **quantity, quality, relation, modality**; e.g. substance, cause, community.
All my representations must be able to be accompanied by **'I think'**: the unity of self-consciousness that requires synthesis by the categories.

Kant's categories and the Transcendental.front: State the core of Kant's Transcendental Deduction
Kant's categories and the Transcendental.back: Unified experience requires **synthesis by rules**; the most general rules are the **categories**; so they apply to **every object of possible experience**, but only to appearances.

Kant's schematism and the Second Analogy.back: A rule translating a category into **time**: substance = **what persists**; cause = **succession according to a rule**.

Kant's schematism and the Second Analogy.front: Kant's ship and house: what is the contrast?
Kant's schematism and the Second Analogy.back: Scanning a **house**, my perceptions can go in any order; watching a **ship** go downstream, the order is **fixed**. Only a causal rule fixes objective succession.

Kant's schematism and the Second Analogy.front: What is Strawson's objection to Kant's Second Analogy?
Kant's schematism and the Second Analogy.back: It slides from **the necessary order of perceptions** (given the event) to **the causal necessity of the event itself**: a non sequitur (*Bounds of Sense*, 1966).

Kant's Refutation of Idealism.back: I am conscious of my existence **as determined in time**; that needs **something permanent**; the permanent cannot be in me; so consciousness of myself is consciousness of **things outside me**.
**Problematic**: outer things doubtful (**Descartes**). **Dogmatic**: outer things denied (**Berkeley**).
Göttingen review of the *Critique* comparing Kant to **Berkeley**; prompted the Refutation added in **1787**.

Kant on phenomena, noumena and the thing.back: **Negative**: what is not an object of our sensible intuition (permitted). **Positive**: an object of intellectual intuition (not available to us).

Kant on phenomena, noumena and the thing.front: Kant's transcendental idealism: two-world versus two-aspect readings
Kant on phenomena, noumena and the thing.back: **Two-world**: appearances and things in themselves are distinct entities. **Two-aspect** (Allison, 1983): one set of things, **considered in two ways**.

Kant on phenomena, noumena and the thing.front: What is Jacobi's objection to Kant's thing in itself?
Kant on phenomena, noumena and the thing.back: Kant says things in themselves **affect** our senses, but **causality** applies only within experience: without it you cannot enter the system, with it you cannot stay.

Kant's paralogisms: the illusion of a kn.back: Reason's natural, unavoidable tendency to treat **ideas of the unconditioned** (soul, world, God) as knowable objects; like the moon looking larger at the horizon.

Kant's paralogisms: the illusion of a kn.front: Kant's diagnosis of the first paralogism
Kant's paralogisms: the illusion of a kn.back: 'Subject' shifts meaning: the **logical subject of thought** (the 'I think') is taken for a **real substance**.
The claim to prove from 'I think' alone that the soul is **substance, simple, identical** through time, and distinct from bodies.

Kant's antinomies of pure reason.back: A pair of opposed claims about **the world as a whole**, each apparently provable. Kant gives **four**.

Kant's antinomies of pure reason.front: Kant's resolution of the mathematical versus the dynamical antinomies
Kant's antinomies of pure reason.back: **Mathematical** (1 and 2): **both sides false**, since the world is never a given whole. **Dynamical** (3 and 4): **both may be true**, of appearances and of things in themselves.
**Thesis**: the world has a beginning in time and limits in space. **Antithesis**: it has no beginning and no limits.

Kant's critique of the proofs of God.front: State Kant's objection to the ontological argument
Kant's critique of the proofs of God.back: **Being is not a real predicate**: existence adds nothing to a concept. 'A hundred real dollars contain no more than a hundred possible dollars.'

Kant's critique of the proofs of God.front: Kant's three possible proofs of God
What is the weakest step in Kant's critique of the proofs of God?
Kant's critique of the proofs of God.back: Many judge it his claim that the **cosmological argument reduces to the ontological**.

Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.front: Kant's *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785)
Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.back: Kant's first book on ethics; Abbott's 1873 translation calls it *Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals*.

Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.front: Kant: what alone is good without qualification?
Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.back: **A good will.** Talents and gifts of fortune can be bad if the will is bad; the good will shines **'like a jewel'** even if it achieves nothing.

Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.front: Kant's shopkeeper: why is his honesty without moral worth?
Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.back: He acts **in accordance with** duty but not **from** duty: **'his own advantage required it'**.

Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.front: What is Schiller's objection to Kant on duty and inclination?
Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w.back: Kant seems to say helping friends **gladly** lacks worth. Reply: Kant asks only what **shows** moral worth, in cases without inclination.

Kant's categorical imperative: the formu.back: **Hypothetical**: if you want X, do Y. **Categorical**: do Y **whatever you want**. Morality is categorical.

Kant's categorical imperative: the formu.front: State Kant's formula of universal law
Kant's categorical imperative: the formu.back: 'Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a **universal law**.' (Abbott, 1873)

Kant's categorical imperative: the formu.front: Why does Kant's false promise fail the universal law test?
Kant's categorical imperative: the formu.back: If everyone made false promises when in need, **no one would accept a promise**: the maxim destroys itself (**contradiction in conception**).

Kant's categorical imperative: the formu.front: What is Hegel's empty-formalism objection to Kant?
Kant's categorical imperative: the formu.back: The universal law test only checks **consistency**; almost any content can be made consistent, so it **cannot say what to do**.

Kant on humanity, autonomy and the kingd.back: Treat humanity, in yourself or another, **always as an end, never merely as a means**.
**Autonomy**: the rational will gives the moral law **to itself**. **Heteronomy**: law grounded in something outside, such as desire or happiness.
